tagline: Ancient crossroads of the Middle East
overview:
Syria sits at the eastern end of the Mediterranean Sea, bordering Turkey, Iraq, Jordan, Israel and Lebanon. It covers about 185,000 km², roughly the size of Washington state, with a green coastal strip, mountains, a wide steppe and desert reaching toward the Euphrates River.

Before 2011 about 21 million people lived in Syria; since then war has displaced more than half the population, and millions live as refugees in neighboring countries and beyond. Arabic is the official language, with Kurdish, Armenian, Syriac and other languages spoken by minority communities. Damascus, the capital, is one of the oldest cities in the world that has been lived in without a break.

Syria is a republic. It has been the site of a civil war since 2011, which has destroyed cities, damaged ancient sites and caused one of the largest humanitarian crises of modern times. The country is now working to recover and rebuild.
landAndNature: A narrow, fertile coastal plain runs along the Mediterranean, backed by the Coastal Mountain Range and, further inland, the Anti-Lebanon Mountains, where Mount Hermon's snow feeds springs. East of the mountains the land dries into steppe and then the Syrian Desert of stone and scrub, crossed by the Euphrates, the country's only major river, which is dammed at Lake Assad. Winters are mild and wet on the coast and cold inland, summers hot and dry. Pistachio, olive and citrus groves cover the west, and wheat and cotton grow along the river. Desert wildlife includes gazelles, striped hyenas and the northern bald ibis, a strange-looking bird whose last wild eastern colony was found near Palmyra.
peopleAndCulture: Syrian food is famous across the Middle East: hummus, tabbouleh, kibbeh, and grilled meats, followed by pastries dripping with syrup and pistachios. Aleppo was known for its soap made from olive and laurel oil and for its enormous covered market, much of it damaged in the fighting. Most Syrians are Arab and Muslim, with Kurdish, Armenian and Assyrian communities and long-established Christian churches where some villagers still speak Aramaic, the language of Jesus. Family gatherings, poetry, backgammon in cafés and strong sweet tea are part of daily life. Syrian craftspeople are known for inlaid woodwork, brocade weaving and glassblowing, skills passed down for centuries in the old cities.
history: Some of the world's first farming villages, writing and alphabets appeared in this region; Ebla and Ugarit kept clay-tablet libraries more than 3,000 years ago. Syria was ruled in turn by Assyrians, Persians, Greeks, Romans, who built the desert caravan city of Palmyra, and Byzantines. After Arab armies arrived in the 630s, Damascus became the capital of the Umayyad caliphate, ruling from Spain to India. Crusaders, Mongols and Ottomans followed; Ottoman rule lasted 400 years. France governed Syria after World War I, and independence came in 1946. Hafez al-Assad took power in 1970 and his son Bashar succeeded him in 2000. Peaceful protests in 2011 were met with force and grew into a civil war involving many armed groups and foreign powers; the Assad government fell in December 2024.
funFacts: Damascus is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities on Earth, with people living there for around 4,000 years or more.
The world's oldest known complete alphabet was found at Ugarit on Syria's coast, written in wedge-shaped signs.
Krak des Chevaliers is one of the best-preserved crusader castles anywhere, with walls up to 30 meters thick in places.
In the village of Maaloula, some people still speak Aramaic, a language spoken in the region 2,000 years ago.
Aleppo soap, made from olive oil and laurel oil and aged for months, has been produced by the same method for centuries.
